title: How to Raise a Son Who Is Boring and Unattractive to Women 7, 2026
author: Anthony Bradley
source: One Little Word / Anthony Bradley's newsletter (anthonybbradley.substack.com), September
summary: Using an ironic 'how to raise a boring son' framing, sociologist Anthony Bradley argues that a specific style of middle-class, résumé-obsessed, single-activity-focused parenting is producing young men who genuinely struggle to hold a conversation, and that this -- not phones, video games, or feminism alone -- may be an underappreciated driver of the dating crisis among Gen Z and Gen Alpha men. He grounds the claim in psychologist Madeline Levine's finding that affluent teens raised purely to perform on résumés were, as a group, simply boring to talk to, and pairs it with Annette Lareau's concept of 'concerted cultivation,' the older middle-class practice of deliberately developing a child's opinions, judgment, and broad cultural exposure rather than narrow achievement in one lane. Bradley traces this to the decline of what he calls WASP culture's expectation that an educated person cultivate taste and social confidence across music, literature, and art, contrasting his own Atlanta childhood -- where every teen boy played both a sport and an instrument -- with today's arts-stripped, single-track school culture. The piece's satirical ten-step 'how to raise a boring son' list (résumé-first activities, cutting out music and the arts, giving him a smartphone as early as possible, isolating him from adult conversation, never asking his opinion) functions as a photo-negative diagnosis of what genuine character and conversational formation actually requires.
points: Bradley locates a specific, testable claim inside a broader dating-crisis debate: rather than blaming phones, games, or feminism in isolation, he proposes narrow-track, résumé-optimized upbringing itself produces young men who are conversationally boring, which independently damages their romantic prospects.

Annette Lareau's 'concerted cultivation' concept is used to name what's been lost: the deliberate, effortful middle-class practice of developing a child's own opinions, judgment, and observational skill, as distinct from merely enrolling them in résumé-building activities.

The anecdote about Christian female college students describing 'nice but incredibly boring' Christian men, several of whom are drawn instead to 'bad boys' because 'they're just more fun,' gives the abstract argument a concrete, uncomfortable social data point.

The satirical ten-step list functions as an inverted diagnostic checklist: each numbered 'how to ruin your son' step (arts removed, opinions suppressed, adult conversation withheld, smartphone given early) names a specific formative input parents can audit and restore rather than a vague cultural complaint.
quotes: Levine noted that these teen clients had one thing in common: they were boring. Raised to perform in school and sports, these teens could not hold interesting conversations about anything.

I've actually had female college students complain to me about this about Christian guys. "They are really nice, but incredibly boring." I had one young woman explain why she and many of her Christian friends were inadvertently drawn to "bad boys.

Middle-class families focused on "developing their children's opinions, judgments, and powers of observation." What I've seen over the years is that with the rise of technocratic parenting, middle-class children have become less likely to learn how to fill 'empty time' with their own creative play, leading them to depend on their parents to solve the problem of boredom.

You want to raise a man. Form his character. Instill curiosity. Give him courage. You'll know you've succeeded when your son can walk into any room and converse with any group of people.
